document_check.note: Gosztolya G, Balogh R, Imre N, Egas-Lopez JV, et al. 'Cross-lingual detection of mild cognitive impairment based on temporal parameters of spontaneous speech', Computer Speech & Language 69 (2021) 101215. It uses two 33-speaker samples (English, New York; Hungarian, Szeged). The cited AUCs of 0.835 and 0.819 match Table 4 (all features, cross-lingual).

cited_result: Cross-lingual SVM classification of MCI vs healthy controls from ASR-derived temporal speech parameters: AUC 0.835 (English speakers, Hungarian ASR) and 0.819 (Hungarian speakers, English ASR), all 15 features, nested speaker-wise cross-validation within each language.
tool_reason: The cited result is the discrimination (AUROC) of a machine-learning classifier built on speech features, so PROBAST with the PROBAST+AI considerations applies.

domains.rationale: This is a small memory-clinic sample. People with depression, stroke, imaging abnormalities or speech disorders were excluded, which narrows the spectrum and removes difficult differential cases (depression also alters speech tempo and pausing). The sampling method is not stated. Discrimination is likely inflated.

signalling.question: 1.1 Were appropriate data sources used?
signalling.answer: Probably yes (clinical recruitment then diagnosis; sampling method not stated)
signalling.quote: A total of 88 elderly individuals were recruited in parallel from two outpatient clinics.

signalling.question: 1.2 Were all inclusions and exclusions of participants appropriate?
signalling.answer: Probably no (exclusion of depression and other conditions narrows the spectrum)
signalling.quote: patients scoring above 10 on GDS-30 or above 5 on GDS-15 were excluded from the study.

domains.rationale: The same recording protocol was used at both sites, features were extracted automatically by ASR after the clinical diagnosis, and speech can be recorded when the model is used. The manual trimming of recordings has minimal potential for bias.

signalling.question: 2.1 Were predictors defined and assessed in a similar way for all participants?
signalling.quote: Each participant’s monologue was recorded by a call recorder application installed on the mobile phone device.

signalling.question: 2.2 Were predictor assessments made without knowledge of outcome data?
signalling.answer: Probably yes (automatic ASR extraction; recordings trimmed manually)
signalling.quote: These utterances were further edited to contain only the speech of the subject (i.e. instructions and possible silent parts before/after his/her speech were removed).

signalling.question: 2.3 Are all predictors available at the time the model is intended to be used?
signalling.quote: A cheap non-invasive way of early screening could be the use of automatic speech analysis.

domains.rationale: The diagnosis used Petersen criteria at memory clinics and was made before the speech recording, so it did not use the predictors. The objective criterion was an MMSE band in the Hungarian sample and is unspecified for the English sample, a limitation that does not change the judgment.

signalling.question: 3.1 Was the outcome determined appropriately?
signalling.quote: This decision was based on Petersen’s criteria (Petersen et al., 1999) in both language groups, with the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE, Folstein et al., 1975) serving as a measure for objective cognitive impairment in the Hungarian-speaking sample (30-28 points: HC; 27-24 points: MCI).

signalling.question: 3.2 Was a pre-specified or standard outcome definition used?
signalling.quote: This decision was based on Petersen’s criteria (Petersen et al., 1999) in both language groups

signalling.question: 3.3 Were predictors excluded from the outcome definition?
signalling.quote: After the clinical evaluation, spontaneous speech samples were obtained from all the participants.

signalling.question: 3.4 Was the outcome defined and determined in a similar way for all participants?
signalling.answer: Probably yes within each language sample
signalling.quote: In all other aspects, the inclusion/exclusion criteria were the same at both sites.

signalling.question: 3.5 Was the outcome determined without knowledge of predictor information?
signalling.quote: After the clinical evaluation, spontaneous speech samples were obtained from all the participants.

signalling.question: 3.6 Was the time interval between predictor assessment and outcome determination appropriate?
signalling.quote: After the clinical evaluation, spontaneous speech samples were obtained from all the participants.

domains.rationale: The validation procedure is sound: nested speaker-wise cross-validation, tuning inside the inner loop, upsampling only in training and a pre-specified feature set. But there are only 13 to 14 MCI cases per sample for 15 predictors (EPV below 1), no confidence intervals and no external validation. The AUCs are therefore very imprecise and prone to overfitting.

signalling.question: 4.1 Were there a reasonable number of participants with the outcome?
signalling.answer: No (14 MCI English, 13 MCI Hungarian, 15 predictors)
signalling.quote: From a machine learning perspective, having fewer than 100 examples (i.e. subjects) is an extremely small dataset.

signalling.question: 4.2 Were continuous and categorical predictors handled appropriately?
signalling.quote: The extracted temporal parameter vectors were standardized before using them in the machine learning step.

signalling.question: 4.3 Were all enrolled participants included in the analysis?
signalling.quote: In the end, a total of 66 subjects were eligible for ﬁnal inclusion.

signalling.question: 4.4 Were participants with missing data handled appropriately?
signalling.quote: After the clinical evaluation, spontaneous speech samples were obtained from all the participants.

signalling.question: 4.5 Was selection of predictors based on univariable analysis avoided?
signalling.quote: hence we calculated 15 temporal parameters overall.

signalling.question: 4.6 Were complexities in the data accounted for appropriately?
signalling.answer: Probably yes (class imbalance addressed in training)
signalling.quote: To balance class distribution during model training, we employed upsampling by repeating examples (i.e. subjects) belonging to the class with fewer examples

signalling.question: 4.7 Were relevant model performance measures evaluated appropriately?
signalling.answer: Probably yes (AUC and Cllr/minCllr; accuracy-type metrics at a threshold set post hoc at EER; no confidence intervals)
signalling.quote: We calculated these values at Equal Error Rate (EER); that is, we chose the decision threshold between the posterior estimates of the two classes (provided by the SVM classiﬁer) in a way which minimizes the absolute difference between the scores sensitivity and speciﬁcity (i.e. recall).

signalling.question: 4.8 Were model overfitting, underfitting and optimism in model performance accounted for?
signalling.answer: Probably yes for tuning optimism (nested CV); precision remains very low
signalling.quote: This way we ensured that we avoided any form of peeking, which would have created a bias in our scores, had we used standard cross-validation.

signalling.question: 4.9 Do predictors and their assigned weights in the final model correspond to the reported multivariable analysis?
signalling.quote: Searched for a reported final SVM model or weights. None reported.

signalling.quote: The meta-parameters of SVM (i.e. C and g) were determined by a technique called nested cross-validation (Cawley and Talbot, 2010).

signalling.quote: This way we ensured that we avoided any form of peeking

signalling.question: AI: Is the reported performance apparent, internally validated or externally validated?
signalling.answer: Internally validated only (nested leave-one-speaker-out within each language); ASR models trained on independent corpora
signalling.quote: Note that, after this step, we still train and evaluate our SVM classiﬁers on subjects belonging only to one language (with the use of the nested cross-validation technique).

overall_rationale: Domain 4 is high because of an extremely small number of events (13 to 14 MCI per sample for 15 predictors, no confidence intervals, no external validation), despite sound nested cross-validation. Domain 1 is high because the exclusion of depression and other conditions narrows the spectrum. Domains 2 and 3 are low.

applicability.rationale: Small memory-clinic samples with depression excluded; the English sample is highly educated (about 17 years of education).
Telephone-recorded spontaneous speech with ASR-derived temporal features, as described in the review.
